chapter_theme: Civakan shoots the boar target on its revolving wheel at Videham, King Govindan proclaims his lineage, a voice from the sky foretells that he will kill Kattiyangaran, Madanan musters the usurper's army, and the poet sets out the two hosts and the opening of the battle, naming its cost in widows, dead beasts and a grieving Earth.

cast.role: the hero, who shoots the boar target at Videham (நம்பன் in 2202)
the king of Videham, who holds the boar contest and proclaims Civakan's lineage; named கோவிந்தன் in 2205
the army assembled at the contest, which roars when the boar falls
the figure who appears in the sky and foretells Kattiyangaran's death
the usurping minister, Civakan's enemy, whose army is counted in 2220
Kattiyangaran's ally, who musters the fourfold army
the hundred spear-bearing sons who gather to the usurper's army
the young warriors who harness the horses and take up arms
the 'learned one' whose spear rages in 2221, probably Civakan
the archers of the two armies
the lancers and swordsmen of the two armies

2202.reading: The boar figure stands on a mortar-shaped head above a turning wheel of red gold set with gems, swinging left and right, and the lord binds the finger-guard, takes up the bow with its arrow, and, the bees in his hair rising, closes on the wheel.
2202.event: Civakan arms himself and goes up to the revolving wheel that carries the boar target.
2202.nuance: The target is a machine: a boar image on a post that swings to either side above a revolving wheel, so the feat is aiming at a moving mark. குப்புற்று (line 4) may mean he leapt or that he bent low; the sense of his approach turns on it.

2203.reading: His diamond ornaments and gem earrings flashing, he wheels round like a whirled firebrand, his gold cord making a circle with the blazing wheel, so that he stands like one sun set upon another.
2203.event: Civakan circles with the turning wheel as he takes aim.
2203.nuance: Each line opens with ஒள்ளழல், 'bright fire', and the verse builds a single figure out of the repetition: the hero, his ornaments and the wheel all become circles of fire, ending in the doubled sun.

2204.reading: With a bow that never breaks, like the rare virtue of penance, a string that never parts, and arrows straight like the minds of the refined, he shoots so that the mechanism and the hard-wrought boar device fall shattered together, he himself like the fire of the world's end joined with thunder.
2204.event: Civakan's arrow strikes the target and shatters both the boar and the machine that moved it.
2204.nuance: The similes borrow from ascetic and moral life: the bow is unbreakable as penance is, the arrows straight as a refined mind. The feat that wins the contest is praised in the language of virtue just before it opens a war. இருந்தவன் பொறியும் (line 3) is obscure; it may name the device on which the boar was mounted.

2205.reading: The bright-tusked boar takes the arrow and crashes to the ground, the drums are beaten with a roar like the troubled sea, the cloud and the gale, the army shouts, and the lord Govindan proclaims the hero's lineage by drum.
2205.event: The boar falls, and King Govindan has Civakan's lineage proclaimed before the assembled host.
2205.nuance: This is the turn of the ilampakam: the contest's winner is named as the dispossessed king's son, so the proclamation of birth is also a declaration of war on the usurper.

2206.reading: A figure appears in the sky and, thundering like a rain cloud, declares that the lion called Civakan, of the honeyed garland and white spear, will swallow the sweet life of the elephant called Kattiyangaran, of the garlanded chest.
2206.event: A voice from the sky foretells that Civakan will kill Kattiyangaran.
2206.nuance: The prophecy is cast as a beast image, lion against elephant, the old figure of the smaller, fiercer animal killing the larger; the next verses give the usurper the larger army.

2207.reading: A speaker scorns the threat: shall he fear because the other has come bringing the fierce army of the Vidyadharas? The other does not know his strength; if it comes to fierce battle, let him cut down that pride and end the deceit, with him.
2207.nuance: No speaker is named. The mention of the Vidyadhara army suits a word aimed at Civakan's side, and the next verse has Madanan blaze up on hearing the 'famed one', so this is read as Kattiyangaran's answer; the closing clause, who is to cut whose pride and whose deceit is meant, can be read either way.

2208.reading: As the sunstone pours out fire on seeing the sun, so Madanan, hearing the word of the far-famed one, blazes up like the thunder of a raining cloud.
2208.event: Madanan flares into rage on hearing the words.
2208.nuance: The sunstone makes the anger borrowed: Madanan's fire is kindled by another's words, as the stone's fire is the sun's. Who the பேரிசையான் is depends on the reading of the previous verse.

2209.reading: In an instant he readies foot soldiers, elephants, horses and chariots and gathers the fourfold army, and a hundred warrior sons with poisoned-leaf spears assemble.
2209.event: Madanan musters the fourfold army, and a hundred spear-bearing sons gather to it.
2209.nuance: Whose sons the hundred are is not said in the verse; the usurper's side is meant.

2210.reading: The poet announces that he will tell all that befell those who met in the sword battle between the fierce army of the master of the bow and the army of the one who rose up in wrath.
2210.nuance: A rare first-person turn by the narrator (உரைக்குற்றேன், line 4), marking the set battle-piece that follows.

2211.reading: The armoured elephants are drawn up in rows, like great jewelled mountains, with forehead plates, rut streaming like falls down their brows, and pearl-bearing tusks that split the front.

2212.reading: As men with curved bows and bloody weapons mount the elephants, the bright flags crowded in the dark sky look like a forest of banners struck by the wind.

2213.reading: The charioteers, with fine cloth on their heads, ready the chariots, beautiful under their parasols, guarded with shields, with raised gold seats and quivers fitted to the footboard.
2213.event: The charioteers make the chariots ready.

2214.reading: They bind the strong yokes with fitted ropes on the trimmed-maned horses and set the goads, and the young men check the bows and other weapons and take them in hand.
2214.event: The young warriors harness the horses and take up their weapons.

2215.reading: The horses, proud and quick as flight, wheel like spinning tops in the wide battle, plumed at the brow, and bear marks on their thighs by which those learned in the great treatises may know where they were bred.
2215.nuance: Line 3 to 4 refer to a learned lore of horses (பெரிய நூலவர்): the breed and country of a horse read from marks on its body.

2216.reading: As Mlecchas mount with deadly-tipped lances, bows and lightning-leaf swords, the horses throng, with gold-meshed caparisons and garlands bounding, raging forward with a roar.
2216.event: Mleccha horsemen mount and the cavalry surges forward.
2216.nuance: Foreign (மிலேச்சர்) horsemen in the army, as in the Sangam memory of Yavana guards; the verse does not say on whose side.

2217.reading: The fierce-eyed foot soldiers have garlands and chaplets on their heads, ringing anklets on their feet, short swords gripped hard in their hands, and mail on their bodies.

2218.reading: The host with its hair-tufted shields, hide shields, long screens, staves and wooden boards in ranks looks like a sea of tigers that has entered the face of battle.

2219.reading: For the one of the kalpaka garland there are war elephants in rut, attended by crowds of spirits and kites, and golden chariots, four and a half kaccham, horses seven lakh, and foot soldiers seven deva-koti, a sea swelling like a rain cloud.
2219.nuance: The verse counts Civakan's army; read with the next it sets the two hosts side by side. The units (கச்சம், இலக்கம், தேவ கோடி) are traditional large numbers and their values are not fixed here.

2220.reading: For Kattiyangaran, then, there were strong chariots with shining-maned horses and fire-wrathful elephants that stoop and gore, five and a half kaccham, horses seven lakh, and foot soldiers seven deva-koti, bright with anklets.
2220.nuance: Against 2219 the usurper's elephants and chariots are one kaccham more, the rest equal: the poem gives the wrongful side the larger force.

2221.reading: So that the women of noble houses put off their adornment, the tossing-maned horses and the elephants die, and the Earth-woman beats her breast with her hand and pines, the learned one raged, and his spear smoked.
2221.event: The fighting begins, its cost foretold in widowed women, dead beasts and a grieving Earth.
2221.nuance: The verse states the war's cost before its glory: widowhood (the noble women's adornment put off), slaughter, and the Earth herself mourning, in an ilampakam named for the Earth-woman (மண்மகள்). Who the புலமகன் is, Civakan or another, the verse does not fix.

2222.reading: Struck with drumsticks, the war drums roar, the white conches and the kettledrums spread their sound, the pampai drums throb, the tall peacock-feather standards rise everywhere, and the din of the front is like the roar of the sea.

2223.reading: The crowned kings are like the rising sun, the massed elephants like great ships breaking the waves, and the flashing swords like killing sharks, so that the clash looks like a time when two seas met in wrath.

2224.reading: Warriors in dark anklets, with quivers packed with arrows tossing on their broad backs and tight girdles, set arrows to their black bows and pour a rain of shafts until the sky is filled.
2224.event: The archers loose a rain of arrows.

2225.reading: Driving their dark arrows into fat-swollen chests, shoulders and foreheads, they fought a tangled battle like men struggling in a fragrant oncoming flood; such was its nature.
2225.event: The armies fight at close quarters with arrows.
2225.nuance: The simile of line 3 sets the slaughter beside the festival play of men and women in scented flood water, a scene the epic elsewhere describes for pleasure.

2226.reading: They drew their burning swords; eyes smoked and burned and lids were scorched; they roared like Death, opened chests and destroyed sweet lives, and the lancers' din grew.

links.note: The prologue's summary joins two acts in one line, that Civakan shot the boar and killed the enemy; 2204 performs the first.
links.teaches: The prologue binds the contest shot to the killing of the usurper, so the reader knows the winning arrow here is the opening blow of the war, not a feat for a bride alone.

links.note: The epic likens the hero's arrows to the straight minds of the refined; the couplet holds that the straight arrow is cruel and that form proves nothing about worth.
links.teaches: Read against the couplet, the simile shows the epic choosing the arrow's straightness as a sign of virtue at the very moment the arrow starts a war of slaughter, which the Kural warns is the arrow's real nature.

gains.a: a check on its own praise: the straight arrow it calls a refined mind is, by the couplet, a killer's shape
gains.b: a case of exactly the misreading it warns against, where an admired shape stands in for goodness in a famous poem

links.note: The epic gives the usurper the larger host, and the couplet says that many steadfast men make no army without leaders.
links.teaches: The counts set Kattiyangaran's bigger force against Civakan's smaller one, so the coming defeat of the larger host turns the couplet's rule about leadership over numbers into a plot.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the counted advantage of the usurper will not decide the battle
gains.b: a story where the two armies are counted unit by unit and the larger one is the one fated to lose

links.note: Both make the Earth a woman on the battlefield: the Kalavazhi's Earth is wrapped red as in a fine cloth by the king's slaughter, the Cintamani's beats her breast and pines.
links.teaches: The same personified Earth that the praise-poem dresses in the victor's blood becomes in the epic a mourner, so the pair shows the one figure serving both the glory and the grief of a war.

gains.a: a sense of how pointed its grieving Earth is, set against the battle-praise convention that adorns her
gains.b: a counter-voice that turns its red-robed Earth from ornament to wound

links.note: The Purananuru poet asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short of ruin when it saw women made widows beat their breasts and shear their hair; the Cintamani names the widows' lost adornment as what the hero's spear will bring.
links.teaches: In the Sangam poem the sight of widows is what checks the spear, while in the epic the widows are counted in advance as the spear's work, so the pair shows grief for the enemy's women moving from a limit on war to its foreseen price.

gains.a: an older measure of a just warrior, who stops at the widows' grief, against which its raging spear is judged
gains.b: a later story where the same grief is foreseen and does not stop the fighting, which sharpens how rare its king's restraint was

links.note: Both set war as a sea with ships: in the epic the two armies meet as two seas with elephants as ships, in the Kalavazhi the blood drags elephants and drums like boats meeting on the sea after the slaughter.
links.teaches: The epic uses the sea at the moment of the clash, the Kalavazhi uses it for the blood that remains after, so together they show the sea image passing from the armies' living mass to the flood of their dead.

gains.a: the aftermath its own image points to: the seas that meet become a sea of blood
gains.b: the moment before its blood-sea, when the boats it shows were the living elephants of two hosts

source_issues: 2202-2206 and 2220 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins read correctly.
2204 line 3 இருந்தவன் பொறியும் is obscure; the reading of what device fell is uncertain.
2207 names no speaker; the attribution to Kattiyangaran rests on context.
2221 line 4 புலமகன் is unexpected and may be a corruption; the agent of the raging spear is uncertain.
